<doc file="docs/advanced/extensions.md" section="`"target"`" lines="141-181">
 141| ### `"target"`
 142| 
 143| The target that is used as [the HTTP target instead of the URL path](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2616#section-5.1.2).
 144| 
 145| This enables support constructing requests that would otherwise be unsupported.
 146| 
 147| * URL paths with non-standard escaping applied.
 148| * Forward proxy requests using an absolute URI.
 149| * Tunneling proxy requests using `CONNECT` with hostname as the target.
 150| * Server-wide `OPTIONS *` requests.
 151| 
 152| Some examples:
 153| 
 154| Using the 'target' extension to send requests without the standard path escaping rules...
 155| 
 156| ```python
 157| # Typically a request to "https://www.example.com/test^path" would
 158| # connect to "www.example.com" and send an HTTP/1.1 request like...
 159| #
 160| # GET /test%5Epath HTTP/1.1
 161| #
 162| # Using the target extension we can include the literal '^'...
 163| #
 164| # GET /test^path HTTP/1.1
 165| #
 166| # Note that requests must still be valid HTTP requests.
 167| # For example including whitespace in the target will raise a `LocalProtocolError`.
 168| extensions = {"target": b"/test^path"}
 169| response = httpx.get("https://www.example.com", extensions=extensions)
 170| ```
 171| 
 172| The `target` extension also allows server-wide `OPTIONS *` requests to be constructed...
 173| 
 174| ```python
 175| # This will send the following request...
 176| #
 177| # CONNECT * HTTP/1.1
 178| extensions = {"target": b"*"}
 179| response = httpx.request("CONNECT", "https://www.example.com", extensions=extensions)
 180| ```
 181|
